reviews.text: This adaptation of Emma Donoghue's 2016 novel centres on Pugh's reliably great performance, though its big reveal does fail to wow.
reviews.author: Francesca Steele

reviews.text: It is a heavy film with tough questions, yet Florence Pugh is up for the challenge as always.
reviews.author: Calum Cooper

reviews.text: A film that fully leans into what makes it work.
reviews.author: Joshua Polanski

reviews.text: The Wonder doesn’t instill “wonder,” nor enjoyment.
reviews.author: Maxance Vincent

reviews.text: Much like the movie sets it depicts in its meta opening, The Wonder is similarly just an empty framework — narrative scaffolding that is never given life and a central purpose by its abridged storytelling.
reviews.author: Prabhjot Bains

reviews.text: Based on Emma Donoghue’s eponymous book, The Wonder is a beautiful yet disturbing psychological thriller with a stellar performance by Florence Pugh.
reviews.author: Mini Anthikad-Chhibber

reviews.text: The Wonder is a mesmerising movie that finds the central character’s unshakable faith being broken and instils curious stories to be investigated.
reviews.author: Nuha Hassan

reviews.text: The Wonder drives its heavy themes home ever so eloquently, resulting in a worthy adaptation that won’t be easy to forget, no fewer thanks to its powerhouse cast.
reviews.author: Anna Miller

reviews.text: The Wonder is a bleak tale of an unexpected connection between two people well acquainted with hardship. Pugh’s performance, as always, elevates this to something beyond a religious period piece mystery about life itself.
reviews.author: Tina Kakadelis

reviews.text: A gritty tale exploring religion vs science that is helmed by a masterful lead performance by Florence Pugh, The Wonder is definitely worth a watch and may nearly pack as much of a punch as the book.
reviews.author: Rebecca Johnson

reviews.text: The sunless landscape that’s being blasted by wind 24×7. The creaking and dreary insides of the houses. The spine-chilling score. The constant glare of kids or elders watching our protagonist. The lack of any warmth between humans. It’s all horror 101.
reviews.author: Pramit Chatterjee

reviews.text: Pugh's performance, which dovetails nicely with newcomer Cassidy’s devout determination as Anna, can’t quite overcome the uneven plotting and, at times, flimsy characterisation.
reviews.author: Amber Wilkinson

reviews.text: Oddly though, the contemporary framing device feels even more superfluous when it returns for the final shot.
reviews.author: Gavia Baker-Whitelaw

reviews.text: Lelio shows an exceptional management of tone and the way he captures and uses his period setting enhances the story in a number of ways. He also knows what he has in Florence Pugh whose standout performance is both thoughtful and haunting.
reviews.author: Keith Garlington

reviews.text: Florence Pugh is perfect in this film by Sebastian Lelio about religious obsession and those skeptical of it.
reviews.author: Santanu Das

reviews.text: The film tacitly frames faith and science as both “stories” with sincere, devoted adherents. But it leaves no doubt as to which story we should prefer.
reviews.author: Brett McCracken

reviews.text: We are left with two possibilities: The Wonder is a deeply cynical artifact, or it's entirely clueless about itself.  It's hard to say which is more depressing.
reviews.author: David Engel

reviews.text: Haunting and atmospheric, director Sebastián Lelio's film operates between faith and evidence.
reviews.author: Kiko Martinez

reviews.text: Lelio (“Disobedience,” “Gloria”) continues his reverence for strong women through Pugh’s haunting portrayal of Lib, a stoic lady who does not suffer fools.
reviews.author: Al Alexander

reviews.text: Florence Pugh confronts uncertainty and skepticism in this piercing drama that questions the power of stories, faith, and freedom. [Full Review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Rene Sanchez

reviews.text: ... an exercise in mood with no visible threats. It will leave you with less than what you demand for a story of this nature.
reviews.author: Filipe Freitas

reviews.text: An adept adaptation of Room author Emma Donoghue’s novel of the same name examines how storytelling can compel, but also conflict, causing further strife amongst those who want to believe in the power of narrative as gospel.
reviews.author: Eric Marchen

reviews.text: The sizable wonder at the center of The Wonder is its star, Florence Pugh. Her perfectly-pitched performance holds together a film that often feels like a horror movie while flirting with questions of faith and the nature of miracles.
reviews.author: Eleanor Ringel Cater

reviews.text: While The Wonder doesn't pack the punch it might have, it's most potent when it reminds us that people's lives can depend on our ways of seeing.
reviews.author: Margot Harrison

reviews.text: The Wonder is honorable, but it’s marred by a particular error. Three times in the film, Lelio reminds us — showing the workings of a film set or having an actor address the camera directly — that the story is a manufactured one.
reviews.author: Steve Murray

reviews.text: A captivating story that oscillates between social realism and the fantastical. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Carlos Bonfil

reviews.text: Pugh gives a great performance, but it's young Cassidy who knocks it out of the park with her full-throated, intensely suffering miracle girl.
reviews.author: Jeffrey M. Anderson

reviews.text: The blessing of The Wonder is how it acknowledges the things we most want to believe and still proposes, in the end, that human acts and faith in others can be the most miraculous things of all.
reviews.author: Sophie Gilbert

reviews.text: While the screenplay has some distractingly pretentious inclinations, it cannot get in the way of a compelling story about the never-ending battle between faith and fact.
reviews.author: Leigh Paatsch

reviews.text: A timely parable about the dangers of unchecked fundamentalism. A “get your kids the damn vaccine” period piece, basically.
reviews.author: Cory Woodroof

reviews.text: A staid drama of a nurse examining a case of breatharianism. Similar to  "The Good Nurse." Both movies examine worlds where some would prefer people die than admit they’d made mistakes. Also another punch to the face of patriarchal societies. Pugh shines.
reviews.author: Mark Jackson

reviews.text: A film with a claustrophobic atmosphere supported by a disquieting score that shows how a good story can gain strength and power over truth, no matter how irrefutable. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Emiliano Basile

reviews.text: The Wonder is a good-looking film, and the performances are engaging and passionate.
reviews.author: Tatat Bunnag

reviews.text: Pugh once again is the only thing drawing our attention in a film that fails to dig below the surface of religion, the patriarchy and medical mystery until it is all but flashing a sign on the screen by the end telling you what it’s big metaphor is.
reviews.author: Erik Childress

reviews.text: It touches on themes of institutionalised religion, the role of women in the 18th century, blind faith and the manipulation of people by spiritual leaders. But it's also an atmospheric experience, starring an awesome Florence Pugh. Full review in Spanish.
reviews.author: Sebastian Zavala Kahn

reviews.text: As a parable of faith versus reason “The Wonder” can be accused of awkwardness and implausibility, but as a portrait of a woman driven to attempt almost anything to save a child from harm it has considerable potency.
reviews.author: Frank Swietek

reviews.text: At last, a movie for which Florence Pugh will do a press tour.
reviews.author: Chance Solem-Pfeifer

reviews.text: This unsettling psychological drama sets reason against piety in a bleak, atmospheric landscape of misty moors.
reviews.author: Whang Yee Ling

reviews.text: Ari Wegner’s cinematography powerfully transported me to this world while also inviting reconsideration of certainty.
reviews.author: Diane Carson

reviews.text: This is an intelligent period piece worth investing the patience required.
reviews.author: Dennis Harvey

reviews.text: Director Sebastian Leilio lets the voice of his well-chosen star (Florence Pugh) ask us to "believe in this story" to begin a hypnotic journey into 1862 Ireland. Methinks you will.
reviews.author: John Urbancich

reviews.text: …The Wonder is an unusual story that may well intrigue, but despite Pugh’s heroic efforts, pivots to a feel-good  conclusion that’s both facile and insulting…
reviews.author: Eddie Harrison

reviews.text: The Wonder is a windswept period piece headlined by Florence Pugh on formidable form. Surrounded by an exceptional company of ensemble players in Toby Jones and Ciaran Hinds amongst others, The Wonder addresses is a film worthy of emotional investment.
reviews.author: Martin Carr

reviews.text: The Wonder is entirely fresh -- and equally brilliant.
reviews.author: Pippa Bailey

reviews.text: The Wonder has demonstrated, powerfully, the ways stories can both sustain us and harm us.
reviews.author: Alison Gillmor

reviews.text: A compelling film with the palette of a painting and the political machinations of The Church from long ago (and of today). By the end, we’re not sure what we want most...but we know the men who wield religion as a scepter cannot be allowed to win.
reviews.author: Sherin Nicole

reviews.text: A worthy companion piece to the recent "She Said" and upcoming "Women Talking," Sebastian Lelio’s "The Wonder" is a powerful social screed that doesn’t suffer from a shortage of ambition.
reviews.author: Charles Koplinski

reviews.text: A compelling drama shorn down to its essentials, both visually and emotionally.
reviews.author: Dwight Brown

reviews.text: Resoundingly dull period twaddle with Pugh’s threadbare performance bordering on stony, the theme of science vs custom underscores the thin story. Yet the big question isn’t what is going on but, well, who cares?
reviews.author: Jim Schembri

reviews.text: The Wonder is a layered examination of our dependence on stories and how we use them. But for all of its sense of spectacle, it lacks any real sense of, well, wonder.
reviews.author: Jess Goodman

reviews.text: A mystery set in 1862 Ireland in which reason is pitted against faith as a nurse tries to figure out a so-called miracle.
reviews.author: Frederic and Mary Ann Brussat

reviews.text: The drama is a mostly compelling watch, but we’re left wanting more from a film with such an impressive assemblage of individual pieces.
reviews.author: Sumner Forbes

reviews.text: Once again Lelio sinks into his female protagonists, a specialty of his, and relies on a performer who plays it to the bone. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Pablo O. Scholz

reviews.text: Pugh gives a wonderful performance in The Wonder, a drama that engages its audience by finding originality in cold, hard truths.
reviews.author: M.N. Miller

reviews.text: A strange, immersive experience involving a devout fasting girl under observation in post-famine Ireland, is told with conviction combining strong central performances and an intriguingly creepy score
reviews.author: Jane Freebury

reviews.text: Lelio directs the film with a steady hand; the cinematography is grand, and there’s a fascinating meta element, a framing story of sorts that feels a little like an afterthought.
reviews.author: Maria Lattila

reviews.text: It satisfies as a well-made psychological thriller.
reviews.author: Dennis Schwartz

reviews.text: It’s a horror movie without the horror.
reviews.author: John McDonald

reviews.text: The power of The Wonder lies in the fact that you are unable to shake off the incidents of the film long after the film has ended.
reviews.author: Abhishek Srivastava

reviews.text: The movie has things to say, things we should all think about. And why not think about those things while watching Pugh give an excellent performance?
reviews.author: Vanessa Armstrong

reviews.text: Pugh is very much at home in this kind of role, but it’s no less arresting in its familiarity.
reviews.author: Clarisse Loughrey

reviews.text: Beneath its satisfying surface mystery, “The Wonder” levels a steady gaze at a faith-ruled culture where the miracles of women are sometimes the only way to cope with the sins of men.
reviews.author: Ty Burr

reviews.text: Behind the dialogue lies one of the favorite themes of Chilean filmmaker Sebastián Lelio: exacerbated, almost mystical, religious devotion, imposed as a mandate for everyday life and a potion capable of replacing the truth. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Marcelo Stiletano

reviews.text: The Wonder is slow-moving, each moment churning into something more cohesive as the film continues, rewarding you at the end. That said, it’s Pugh’s performance that solidifies this film as a contender this year.
reviews.author: Kate Sánchez

reviews.text: Pugh brings so much pent-up emotion to Lib, it’s impossible not to be drawn into her struggle. Come for the murky landscape but stay for yet another worthy Pugh performance.
reviews.author: Steven Prokopy

reviews.text: The Wonder is a film that requires patience and understanding, but the fascination of what Anna is going through may captivate audiences from the start. The pacing doesn’t fully work, but Pugh and Cassidy are excellent.
reviews.author: Austin Burke

reviews.text: Divinity and depravity collide in director Sebastian Lelio’s The Wonder. It’s the second Netflix film in less than a month, after The Good Nurse, to be thoroughly misrepresented by its mid title.
reviews.author: Rohan Naahar

reviews.text: This movie forces the viewer to watch, an act many of us take for granted. Many viewers may turn off after the first thirty minutes, but it will be a success for those willing to stay vigilant until the end.
reviews.author: Alex Maidy

reviews.text: The Wonder is an amazing film that delivers an emotionally powerful story of faith and some of the most beautiful images set to screen this year.
reviews.author: Kyle Logan

reviews.text: A child’s survival without food is a miracle waiting to happen for believers and a minefield of secrets for the sceptical.
reviews.author: Andiee Paviour

reviews.text: While The Wonder does get a little too focused on atmosphere and ambiguity for its own good, Sebastián Lelio still orchestrates a compelling blend of character study and moral drama.
reviews.author: Marshall Shaffer

reviews.text: Anchoring the film is Pugh, who brings a youthful earnestness and no-nonsense quality to Lib.
reviews.author: Loren King

reviews.text: The film as a whole, however, is more than the sum of its stunning parts -- nothing short of a comment on how we all find meaning in the world.
reviews.author: Chloe Schama

reviews.text: A fiction about fiction that's unashamed of its narrative identity. And that's its biggest merit. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Randy Meeks

reviews.text: [A] perverse, provocative story about women, their appetites and a world that barbarically tries to control them both.
reviews.author: Manohla Dargis

reviews.text: It was a stellar performance by Pugh but the movie as a whole is a quiet attack on you and when you realize what is happening, you’re stuck just in awe of how the writing of Alice Birch and the direction of Sebastián Lelio got us here.
reviews.author: Rachel Leishman

reviews.text: The Wonder quietly resonates; it’s an idiosyncratic film, but a sturdy one.
reviews.author: Sean Collier

reviews.text: The Wonder will test the patience of people with short attention spans, but the movie's subtlety, nuances, and Florence Pugh's standout performance are great rewards for people who want to see a drama about religion and moral hypocrisy.
reviews.author: Carla Hay

reviews.text: The Wonder crosses a line between eerie ambiguity and aimless floundering.
reviews.author: Katie Rife

reviews.text: Hailed after several festival showings as a “slow burn,” it’s more like trying to light a pile of sodden wood.
reviews.author: Daniel M. Kimmel

reviews.text: An intense, poignant, and deeply moving examination of faith, science, grief, and the dangers of extreme piety at a terrible cost.
reviews.author: Shannon Connellan

reviews.text: Not every story can or should be a movie, despite Hollywood’s insistence otherwise. Some should remain books. Some should remain silent. And some, such as this, provide a fresh reminder of the power of visual storytelling.
reviews.author: John Anderson

reviews.text: The four essences of The Wonder reside in its ambiguous denouement: compassion, prohibition, confusion, and expiation. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Javier Ocaña

reviews.text: Pugh carries The Wonder when it threatens to buckle under lofty ideas that it's reticent to explore with the fervor its subject matter would call for.
reviews.author: Graeme Guttmann

reviews.text: The gimmick turns out to be an inconsequential and hollow one, but the story itself is worth taking seriously and with some serious thought.
reviews.author: Mark Dujsik

reviews.text: An eerie drama of blind faith, religion, scepticism and uncertainty.
reviews.author: Casey Chong

reviews.text: An investigation into the fictions people tell themselves to survive terrible times.
reviews.author: Alistair Harkness

reviews.text: Despite its strong sense of atmosphere and an intense performance by lead actress Florence Pugh, it’s strangely uninvolving.
reviews.author: James Berardinelli

reviews.text: Set designs and costuming are well crafted, and while the self-awareness of the script is a risk, it does provide a unique opportunity to call direct attention to what’s believable.
reviews.author: Chris Joyce

reviews.text: The Wonder is a bleak and desperately haunting story of oppressive religious faith. Florence Pugh delivers a thoughtful and compassionate performance as a weary protagonist searching for the truth.
reviews.author: Julian Roman

reviews.text: It makes simplicity its best asset and continues to be majestic. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Janire Zurbano

reviews.text: Largely thanks to Pugh, Leilo’s semi-experimental attempt at blending an old-fashioned melodrama with Media Studies 101 commentary never makes you feel like you’re watching something created in a dorm-session smokeout.
reviews.author: David Fear

reviews.text: What makes The Wonder feel callous and biased in its investigation, however, is its fealty to an anti-Irish sentiment that drove one million citizens to starvation during a 10-year period.
reviews.author: Natalia Keogan

reviews.text: Florence Pugh gives another scorching performance.
reviews.author: Mike McGranaghan

reviews.text: Once you've broken through the icy exterior, and if you can get past the distracting meta-framing device, there's plenty to reward you here.
reviews.author: Alistair Ryder

reviews.text: Lelio has gifted Pugh with a role that is likely to prove as definitive in her career. Even as the film earns its title from the would-be wonder of the miracle child, it offers us its own wonder of Florence Pugh’s interminable gifts as a performer.
reviews.author: Andrew Kendall

reviews.text: A tony, if not entirely persuasive drama about faith and science in 19th-Century rural Ireland, The Wonder is energized by Florence Pugh’s performance.
reviews.author: Liam Lacey

reviews.text: Much like the lead character, The Wonder is asking the audience to be patient, to figure out exactly what is at hand, and fight the struggle of doing what is right when you are a lone voice in a crowd.
reviews.author: Leo Brady

reviews.text: Magnetic, haunting and captivating... an exquisitely led picture, and cast all-round.
reviews.author: Sarah Ward

reviews.text: If this film is nominated, I will not be surprised, particularly when it comes to cinematography...
reviews.author: Stephen Romei

reviews.text: If you watch with patience, compromise, attention, generosity, and all the senses, The Wonder is a slow-burning work of art that will reward you with a hypnotic experience. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Diego Batlle

reviews.text: It’s a hefty opening note, promising a degree of intrigue that lands more superficially than likely intended. Still, that shouldn’t be held too much against it — across the board, The Wonder proves to be an engrossing effort.
reviews.author: Travis DeShong

reviews.text: The lighting and composition is such that practically every frame could be hung in the National Gallery.
reviews.author: Brian Viner

reviews.text: The Wonder has a weird, hypnotic tenor about it that you don’t expect but is hugely refreshing.
reviews.author: Hilary A White

reviews.text: This film's slow-burn pace --which won't work for everyone -- had me entirely hooked. [Florence Pugh is] as mesmerising here as she's ever been, delivering on this haunting, unsettling, and engrossing story.
reviews.author: Kate Rodger

reviews.text: Basically, the film is a waiting game, with Lelio, a sophisticated technician, using every available trick to keep us engaged... Mainly what we’re asked to do is keep watch on Pugh, who is equipped to make Lib into a mystery in her own right.
reviews.author: Jake Wilson

reviews.text: Unfortunately, outside of Pugh, The Wonder underwhelms.
reviews.author: Soham Gadre

reviews.text: What I like best about “The Wonder” and Pugh’s performance is the contrast of the modern-thinking, intelligent and educated nurse and the closed-minded, almost medieval villagers whose “faith” defies any modern logic.
reviews.author: Robin Clifford

reviews.text: The Wonder coheres as a powerful study of the way in which people are cloistered by their own stories.
reviews.author: Josh Wise

reviews.text: Equally haunting, heartbreaking and heartening, it’s a narrative about narratives’ ability to transform, destroy, resurrect, imprison, and liberate.
reviews.author: Nick Schager

reviews.text: Pugh’s performance as Lib is the magnetic force at the heart of the film’s success. She reveals Lib’s complexities in a slow but powerful burn, unfurling humour and warmth from beneath the sceptical and world-weary exterior of her character.
reviews.author: Rachel Ashby

reviews.text: The compelling work from Pugh and newcomer Cassidy provides more than enough intrigue in the movie’s strongest moments.
reviews.author: Aaron Neuwirth

reviews.text: A rare misfire from director Sebastián Lelio, whose approach to his tale of a 19th century English nurse (Florence Pugh) investigating an Irish miracle is far too plain to be mysterious or stirring.
reviews.author: Siddhant Adlakha

reviews.text: There’s a deep emotional seam that runs through The Wonder which viscerally challenges your preconceptions of faith, morality and care.
reviews.author: Wenlei Ma

reviews.text: The holes in this thing are evident from the very beginning... There's no real mystery.
reviews.author: Wade Major

reviews.text: It's an interesting and compelling premise, but it feels pretty dull and empty.
reviews.author: Claudia Puig

reviews.text: Finds a very human way into a conversation about how we measure and value truth.
reviews.author: Radheyan Simonpillai

reviews.text: Sebastián Lelio continues his streak of films about strong women facing societal obstacles, this time a period piece based on a novel by "Room's" Emma Donoghue where science is pitted against religious beliefs in a contest of grieving mothers.
reviews.author: Laura Clifford

reviews.text: The Wonder is a fine piece of period storytelling.
reviews.author: Paul Whitington

reviews.text: A unique and well-executed film, The Wonder is surprisingly optimistic despite the dark subject matter and an engrossing watch to boot.
reviews.author: Gemma Creagh

reviews.text: A clever prestige project whose neat assembly of themes and talent can sometimes seem to have started in a flat-pack.
reviews.author: Danny Leigh

reviews.text: Florence Pugh's best performance to date..the idea that the Roman Catholic church's influence is manipulated within an entire community seems preposterous, but that's the genius of the thing.
reviews.author: Anne Brodie

reviews.text: Science and belief clashes aside, The Wonder is a transfixing, transportive film, anchored by the incomparable Pugh.
reviews.author: Lindsey Bahr

reviews.text: Wonder's spare, muted intrigue hangs mostly on Pugh and atmosphere, an elusive minor-key mystery.
reviews.author: Leah Greenblatt

reviews.text: Thanks to a typically mesmerizing leading turn from Florence Pugh, it’s a film that can hold up a mirror to believers and nonbelievers alike as the best stories of faith do.
reviews.author: Jack Smart

reviews.text: Pugh’s performance is all-business, like a 19th-century Dana Scully in a town full of Mulders.
reviews.author: Johnny Oleksinski

reviews.text: It’s a performance that, if there’s any justice, should certainly put [Pugh] in the frame for plenty of accolades during the upcoming awards season.
reviews.author: James Croot

reviews.text: Florence Pugh delivers greatness and gravitas as 19th century English nurse investigating a miracle in Scottish countryside.
reviews.author: James Verniere

reviews.text: Well-portrayed by Pugh and Cassidy, which drives this film to unexpected destinations.
reviews.author: Randy Myers

reviews.text: ... a quietly powerful and deeply intriguing look at zealotry and oppression that nourishes both the eyes and the brain.
reviews.author: Todd Jorgenson

reviews.text: Somewhat bizarrely, the film is bookended with a breaking of the fourth wall. But ignore this and you'll be rewarded with a narrative that explores a fascinating territory with a deft, yet capable touch.
reviews.author: Stefan Pape

reviews.text: A drama this ambitious demands a fearless performer like Florence Pugh, who knows exactly the tightrope to walk when it comes to the story’s delicate balance between realism and melodrama.
reviews.author: Brian Tallerico

reviews.text: Pugh’s sensuality, passion and human sympathy are the driving forces of a movie which might otherwise teeter under the weight of its contrivances...
reviews.author: Peter Bradshaw

reviews.text: “The Wonder” undeniably resonates in these confounding times concerning belief, fact and manipulation.
reviews.author: Robert Abele

reviews.text: Imbued with an exceptional performance by Florence Pugh, “The Wonder” is undone by an empty and middling framing device.
reviews.author: Nate Adams

reviews.text: Forcing yourself to watch movies until the end isn’t your job, is it? So there’s no reason for you to sit through a film that feels like work and that leaves you with very little.
reviews.author: Mick LaSalle

reviews.text: Few will remain unmoved by this intriguingly adventurous and thought-provoking drama.
reviews.author: Mark Kermode

reviews.text: The Wonder is just that. A gripping gothic morality tale on the power of blind faith. Impeccably acted and quietly moving. Believe.
reviews.author: Matt Rodgers

reviews.text: The Wonder a haunting, beguiling proposition whose unwinding slow build is certainly worth the ultimate pay off.
reviews.author: Chris Connor

reviews.text: So even if the disparate elements of the overall piece don’t quite come together into a wholly meaningful tapestry, each strand is nevertheless adorned with its own separate wonder.
reviews.author: Christopher Llewellyn Reed

reviews.text: Lelio skilfully balances his characters and options until the very end, infusing the story with a great deal more drama than the premise suggests; Tom Burke and Toby Jones stand out amongst a solid cast; but... Pugh is the bedrock.
reviews.author: Demetrios Matheou

reviews.text: Missteps badly here in such a way that it derails an unbelievable-but-true story about the nature of miracles.
reviews.author: Travis Hopson

reviews.text: It is the cast and the sensitive direction by the filmmaker that makes possible this singular, highly personal depiction of what might be called either an unusual love story or a beautiful and ingenious rescue tale.
reviews.author: Monica Reid

reviews.text: It all ultimately feels like a lot of atmosphere that doesn’t lead anywhere, with themes and metaphors that are so obvious they sap tension.
reviews.author: Steph Green

reviews.text: The Wonder grows in power as it tenderly unfolds the complex worlds, wounds and stories inside its characters with captivating insight.
reviews.author: Katherine McLaughlin

reviews.text: It’s Pugh and Cassidy who are especially remarkable in this story of faith versus science, and a strong-willed woman trying to do the right thing in a man’s world.
reviews.author: Anna Smith

reviews.text: The Wonder is a beautifully shot, enthralling thriller that explores the conflict between fact and faith. Florence Pugh gives another phenomenal performance, holding the audience in the palm of her hand the entire time.
reviews.author: Lauren Bradshaw

reviews.text: F lorence Pugh’s acting is the miracle we take for granted.
reviews.author: Charlotte O'Sullivan

reviews.text: It might have all been too weighty and metaphorical were it not for Pugh... She is the whole package. A wonder indeed.
reviews.author: Kevin Maher

reviews.text: Entrancing and subtly atmospheric, with stellar performances from Pugh and Cassidy.
reviews.author: Katie Smith-Wong

reviews.text: Pugh is riveting: she makes you feel Lib’s mind pushing at the walls of this bizarre scenario, scratching for the chink in the fiction that will lead her to truth.
reviews.author: Robbie Collin

reviews.text: I can't shake the feeling, however, that The Wonder has pulled a lot of punches to be more likable when it'll only ever be as likable as a film like this can be...
reviews.author: Walter Chaw

reviews.text: Pugh gives some of the best work of her already impressive career, reminding audiences how excellently well-suited she is for period dramas as she was in “Lady Macbeth” and “Little Women.”
reviews.author: Nicole Ackman

reviews.text: Pugh disappears into the time period and her character effortlessly, while still maintaining an air of modernity that prevents 19th century England from becoming stale.
reviews.author: Rachel Ho

reviews.text: The team behind "The Wonder" spins a sinuous narrative of many colors. It’s easily one of the classiest films that Netflix has distributed.
reviews.author: Kent Turner

reviews.text: It’s a shame that The Wonder seems distrustful of its audience because Pugh does such a great job and everything in-between this framing device is intriguing, beautifully shot, and restrained.
reviews.author: Kayleigh Donaldson

reviews.text: An alluring tale that’s rich in atmosphere and hooks near-immediately with its central premise.
reviews.author: Peter Gray

reviews.text: ...it’s difficult, ultimately, not to wonder what drew Lelio to this run-of-the-mill, underwhelming material in the first place.
reviews.author: David Nusair

reviews.text: The film is an utterly magnetic examination of narratives, how they take hold and how ultimately, what gives them their power is whether or not we choose to believe in them.
reviews.author: Gayle Sequeira

reviews.text: Lelio has always been a talented filmmaker with a unique creative flare, and The Wonder is no exception.
reviews.author: Wilson Kwong

reviews.text: "The Wonder" remains interested in the immense suffering felt by its characters at the hands of a draconian religion, and is not terribly taken by their humanity.
reviews.author: Robert Daniels

reviews.text: All that makes it unwieldy also makes The Wonder mesmerizing so that, even when the spell is broken, you can’t shake it from your mind.
reviews.author: Chase Hutchinson

reviews.text: A film about the danger of believing without questioning that turns us into full-throated believers in whatever Lelio and Pugh can do.
reviews.author: Benjamin Lee

reviews.text: Leilo’s film is really focused on The Nurse, played by Pugh. She works through pretty much every emotional and intellectual string of what is happening to this young girl. I expect Pugh to be Oscar-nominated for this work.
reviews.author: David Poland

reviews.text: As the picture develops from a spooky Brontë romance into a pointed indictment of society, it takes aim at some familiar targets, but the dramatic impact is powerful.
reviews.author: Kyle Smith

reviews.text: As its Brechtian magic-trick framing device makes clear, “The Wonder” understands storytelling itself to be an act of faith — on the part of the storyteller and their audiences.
reviews.author: Justin Chang

reviews.text: The Wonder is an effective period thriller that, while not reinventing the wheel of the genre, compels you from the start and leaves you invested till the end.
reviews.author: Ryan McQuade

reviews.text: Atmospheric and intriguing up to a point, it nonetheless feels like much ado about a mildly curious situation that’s been milked for rather more than it’s worth.
reviews.author: Todd McCarthy

reviews.text: An illuminating study of dark prejudices.
reviews.author: Stephen Farber

reviews.text: There couldn’t have been a more fitting match between the curiosities of an author and filmmaker.
reviews.author: Tomris Laffly

reviews.text: Lelio has a way with his actors. Nothing will ever feel forced. Even the most melodramatic stakes will feel grounded. And yet, despite a pointless framing device the film simply does not need, it’s missing some of the visual magic of his earlier films.
reviews.author: Gregory Ellwood

reviews.text: An evenhanded but ultimately preposterous adaptation of Emma Donoghue’s novel, co-written by the author herself (with an assist from Alice Birch).
reviews.author: Peter Debruge

reviews.text: The Wonder often skims along the surface when it should cut deeper, but the film’s obviousness only holds it back for so long. By the time it reaches its final shot, you just might believe every word of it, too.
reviews.author: David Ehrlich

synopsis: The Irish Midlands, 1862 -- a young girl stops eating but remains miraculously alive and well. English nurse Lib Wright is brought to a tiny village to observe eleven-year old Anna O'Donnell. Tourists and pilgrims mass to witness the girl who is said to have survived without food for months. Is the village harboring a saint 'surviving on manna from heaven' or are there more ominous motives at work? A psychological thriller inspired by the 19th century phenomenon of the "fasting girls" and adapted from the acclaimed novel by Emma Donoghue (Room).
